title: Newsom moves to commute all California death sentences
rawText:
California death row sentences to be commuted to life without parole, Newsom says
Gov. Gavin Newsom says he will commute every current death sentence in California to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
Newsom announced the decision Thursday in an open letter, saying he will use his constitutional clemency authority to commute the sentences of 548 people currently facing the death penalty.
"I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us," Newsom wrote.
The move does not repeal California's death penalty or prevent prosecutors from seeking it in future cases. Newsom said those decisions will remain with prosecutors, juries and courts.
"Many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die. But as Governor, I have concluded the state cannot morally kill them," Newsom wrote.
California voters, however, have repeatedly chosen to keep the death penalty.
Voters rejected Proposition 34, which would have abolished capital punishment, in 2012. Four years later, they again rejected repeal with Proposition 62 while narrowly approving Proposition 66, which sought to speed up death penalty cases.
Newsom imposed a moratorium on executions shortly after taking office in 2019. California last carried out an execution in 2006.
The decision drew sharply different reactions from California criminal justice officials.
Los Angeles County Public Defender Ricardo García praised the move, saying his office had called for universal clemency because of what he described as deep inequities in the death penalty system.
"Clemency is not leniency," García said in a statement. "This decision moves California closer to a justice system that values human dignity."
Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer strongly criticized the commutations, saying they override verdicts reached by juries and undermine the wishes of crime victims' families.
"The pursuit of justice does not bend to political whims, and I am heartbroken for the hundreds of families who must now grapple with the devastation of knowing that the monsters who harmed their loved ones are one step closer to being back out on our streets," Spitzer stated.
Spitzer said his office will continue seeking the death penalty in cases where prosecutors believe it is warranted.
Under the commutations announced Thursday, every current death sentence would instead become life without parole, which Newsom called the most severe punishment he can impose through clemency.
Some cases will require review by the California Supreme Court because the state constitution requires court approval before a governor can grant clemency to someone convicted of more than one felony.

title: Por qué el Congreso de Paraguay no aceptó la renuncia de Santiago Peña como presidente y qué supone ahora el juicio político en su contra
rawText:
Por qué el Congreso de Paraguay no aceptó la renuncia de Santiago Peña como presidente y qué supone ahora el juicio político en su contra
La crisis política abierta en Paraguay con la renuncia este jueves del presidente Santiago Peña por el escándalo en torno a la intervención de uno de los principales bancos del país vivió un capítulo inesperado cuando el Congreso decidió no aceptarla.
Pese a ser rivales de Peña, los congresistas opositores votaron en contra de aceptar su renuncia para evitar que obtuviera fuero constitucional como expresidente y senador vitalicio.
La decisión final sobre este punto quedó congelada por falta de quorum, después de que algunos legisladores abandonaran la sesión antes de votar.
Un grupo de senadores de la oposición y del propio partido de Peña, el Partido Colorado, impulsaba en cambio un procedimiento de juicio político para destituirlo.
En una jornada en la que se produjeron enfrentamientos en los exteriores del Congreso y en medio de rumores sobre una posible salida del país, Peña anunció en un mensaje en X su intención de presentarse en el juicio y ejercer su defensa.
"Colaboraré plenamente con las instituciones competentes para que se esclarezca lo ocurrido, se determinen las responsabilidades y quienes hayan infringido la ley respondan ante la Justicia", indicó Peña.
Poco después, el vocero presidencial, Guillermo Grance, aseguró que Peña se encuentra en su residencia.
Por qué renunció Peña
Peña presentó su renuncia este jueves en medio del escándalo en torno a Ueno Bank, uno de los principales bancos del país, que fue intervenido el martes por el Banco Central del Paraguay tras haberse detectado que no alcanzaba los mínimos legales de solvencia.
Cerca de tres millones de clientes se quedaron sin acceso a su dinero y las protestas en la calle no se hicieron esperar.
"He tomado la decisión de presentar mi renuncia a la presidencia de la República. Lo hago pensando en la estabilidad de nuestro país, en la paz social y en la necesidad de preservar nuestras instituciones democráticas", comunicó Peña en un mensaje de video que difundió en sus redes sociales.
El presidente, que asumió el cargo en agosto de 2023, expresó su deseo de que se garantice la devolución de los depósitos y se protejan los fondos públicos afectados.
Peña era accionista del grupo propietario de la entidad hasta el año pasado.
Hacia el juicio político
Poco después de que presentara su renuncia, la Cámara de Diputados aprobó la apertura de un juicio político a Peña con los votos de los representantes de su propio partido.
Antes de procesar el juicio político, el Congreso abrió una sesión conjunta de diputados y senadores para votar si aceptaba la renuncia de Peña.
Pero cuando los legisladores estaban emitiendo su voto, los diputados del Partido Colorado -al que pertenece Peña- abandonaron el pleno y se decretó la falta de quórum.
El acuerdo de las bancadas en el Congreso fue que el Senado procesara el juicio político abierto por los diputados más temprano con el que se decidirá si el presidente es destituido para enfrentar las acusaciones de la Fiscalía.
Esto dejó sin efecto la renuncia del presidente, que se mantiene en el cargo.
La decisión de los legisladores de la oposición de rechazar la renuncia de Peña puede parecer paradójica a primera vista, pero se explica por los procedimientos que prevén las leyes paraguayas.
Si el Congreso hubiera aceptado su renuncia, Peña se habría convertido automáticamente en senador vitalicio y disfrutaría, por tanto, de un fuero que dificultaría la persecución penal inmediata iniciada por la Fiscalía.
Despojarle del fuero requeriría del voto de una mayoría parlamentaria.
Al optar por la continuidad del juicio político, el Congreso facilita que Peña sea eventualmente acusado por sus presuntas responsabilidades en el caso Ueno Bank.
De qué se acusa a Peña
A Peña se lo señala, sobre todo, por un presunto conflicto de intereses por sus vínculos con el conglomerado que gestiona Ueno Bank.
Estos son los puntos principales de la acusación:
- Conflicto de intereses y vínculos con Ueno Holding SAECA / Ueno Bank: Peña tuvo acciones millonarias en la sociedad hasta 2025 (dos años después de asumir la presidencia) y se le cuestionan algunos de los nombramientos de funcionarios en la entidad financiera.
- Crisis y colapso financiero de Ueno Bank: después de la intervención de la entidad por el Banco Central del Paraguay (BCP) se señaló a Peña por el impacto en la confianza en el sistema financiero y que cientos de miles de ahorristas se quedaran sin acceso a sus depósitos.
- Injerencia en el Instituto de Previsión Social (IPS): se acusa a Peña de una intervención indebida en el IPS —organismo que administra las jubilaciones y la salud de los trabajadores— para colocar fondos en Ueno Bank.
- Beneficio patrimonial e indicios de enriquecimiento ilícito: se apunta a un presunto beneficio indebido del mandatario, incluidos préstamos recibidos del banco y denuncias previas vinculadas a su patrimonio.
- Responsabilidad institucional y contexto político: la acusación también incorpora cuestionamientos por decisiones y omisiones políticas de su gestión.
Derecho a la defensa
Si dos terceras partes de los senadores (30 votos de 45) aceptan la destitución, Peña podrá quedar expuesto a un posible procesamiento penal sin que sea necesario iniciar un procedimiento de desafuero por su condición de senador vitalicio.
Así, la decisión de los senadores no solo definirá el desenlace de la crisis política, sino que también marca el horizonte jurídico que enfrentará el mandatario tras dejar la Presidencia.
El propio Peña indicó en un mensaje en X que respondería a las acusaciones.
"Ante la continuidad del juicio político, me presentaré y ejerceré mi derecho a la defensa. Lo haré con argumentos y pruebas, con respeto a la Constitución y a las instituciones de la República", escribió el presidente antes de que los senadores abrieran la sesión.

title: La finca inglesa de más de 2400 hectáreas que Salvador Dalí transformó en surrealista
rawText:
Monkton House es un cottage situado en Sussex, Inglaterra, que fue construido entre 1902 y 1903
- 4 minutos de lectura'
Salvador Dalí, una de las figuras más emblemáticas del surrealismo, dejó su huella tanto en la pintura como en la intervención de espacios arquitectónicos. Entre los más célebres se encuentran su residencia en Cadaqués, donde vivió durante años, y el teatro de Figueres, que hoy alberga buena parte de su producción artística. Sin embargo, lejos del Mediterráneo existe otra obra vinculada al artista que suele pasar inadvertida.
Se trata de Monkton House, un cottage situado en Sussex, Inglaterra, que poco tiene de convencional. Construido entre 1902 y 1903 por el arquitecto Edwin Lutyens para el reconocido empresario William Dodge James, fue su único hijo, Edward, quien impulsó su conversión en un ícono del surrealismo. Apasionado coleccionista de este movimiento, en 1930 dio inicio a la transformación de la tradicional residencia inglesa, dentro de su finca de más de 2400 hectáreas.
El heredero comenzó a llenar las salas de su hogar con diferentes artículos y artefactos diseñados por Salvador Dalí. Redefinió el estilo de la época, agregando un toque poco convencional y revolucionario. Desde sillones con la forma de los labios de Mae West hasta desagües que imitaban cañas de bambú, la casa lo tenía todo.
“Es el mejor interior que sobrevivió en este país”, declaró al New York Times Clive Aslet, historiador de arquitectura: “No hay nada en Inglaterra que se compare a Monkton”.
El fanático del surrealismo puso un freno a las ideas de Dalí y descartó que las paredes del salón se movieran hacia adentro y hacia afuera como el estómago de un perro. Aún así, el hogar conserva cientos de elementos sorprendentes. La fachada ya indica que la casa no es una simple vivienda campestre: un color morado tapa el antiguo ladrillo, y unas cortinas de yeso sobresalen por debajo de las ventanas de ambos lados.
Pero lo que más resalta es su interior. La cama del cuarto principal está inspirada en el boceto del coche fúnebre de Napoleón, y el baño está construido con alabastro, una piedra blanda y translúcida utilizada en la escultura, ideal para colocar imágenes brillantes del sol y la luna.
El artista abandonó sus distintivos toques del Mediterráneo y se adaptó completamente a la cultura inglesa. Las chimeneas poseen un estilo Regencia, las paredes del salón y del comedor se tapizaron con lino gris imitando la forma de un sillón victoriano, y la escalera se alfombró primero con las imágenes de los pies de la mujer de Sir Edward James, y tras su divorcio se rediseñó para que aparezcan las huellas de sus perros.
Mark Girouard, también historiador de arquitectura, se refirió a Monkton como “una pequeña obra de arte... Ingeniosa, creativa, cautivadora y totalmente diferente a cualquier otro lugar que haya visto”.
Tras la muerte de Edward, la finca quedó como propiedad de su fundación, que luego la vendió a un comprador privado. English Heritage, una organización que protege el patrimonio histórico del país, quiso recuperarla sin éxito. El nuevo propietario quitó los objetos característicos de su interior, pero conservó la fachada intacta.
El hogar de Salvador Dalí en Cadaqués
En Portlligat, a cinco kilómetros de Cadaqués, se alza la Casa Museo Salvador Dalí. El artista eligió su hogar en 1930 y lo construyó en una zona donde había un grupo de cabañas de pescadores. Fue su residencia hasta 1982, el año de la muerte de su esposa.
Este espacio conserva intacto el espíritu del artista: cuenta con su taller donde pintó varias de sus obras icónicas, pequeños pasillos laberínticos y un oso polar en la entrada que recibe a los invitados.

title: Horóscopo Acuario de hoy, 06 de noviembre de 2026: las predicciones para la salud, el amor y el dinero
rawText:
Conocé las predicciones y qué le depara el horóscopo a Acuario este viernes 06 de noviembre de 2026 en cuestiones de salud, amor y dinero.
A Acuario le fascina lo raro, lo exótico, lo diferente, lo novedoso y lo distinto; siempre tiene que “dar la nota”. Es rápido, inteligente, independiente y sociable y tiene mucha visión de futuro, aunque a veces le cuesta el “aquí y ahora”. Es bueno para trabajar en equipo aunque es individualista y desapegado. Le gusta lo híper-moderno y, aunque no lo podamos creer, tiene muy claro el valor del dinero y es muy ahorrativo.
Qué le espera a Acuario el viernes 06 de noviembre
Renueva tu espíritu y estado anímico, esto te dará seguridad y te permitirá ganar respeto y confianza ante los demás.
Salud: Tu búsqueda constante de la verdad te llevará a tropezar con la misma piedra más de una vez. Aprende de esas caídas y quédate con lo bueno.
Amor: Tu pareja tiene el corazón cerrado para ti, pero no dejes que otro se apodere de tu pasión. Di un no rotundo.
Dinero: Tu mente fría, racionalista, seria y calculadora se pone al servicio de tu ambición, y los dividendos no tardarán en llegar.
Acuario es el décimo primer signo del zodíaco. Su elemento es el aire, al igual que el de Géminis y Libra. Pertenecen al signo de Acuario las personas nacidas entre el 21 de enero y el 19 de febrero.

title: Judge blocks construction on Trump’s D.C.-area arch after commission’s approval
rawText:
A federal judge late Thursday temporarily blocked construction on President Donald Trump’s “Triumphal Arch” shortly after a planning commission led by Trump appointees approved it.
U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan granted a temporary restraining order blocking the administration from “initiating, making, or otherwise effectuating any construction, excavation” or other steps in the arch project for 14 days.
Chutkan’s order came within an hour of the National Capital Planning Commission’s approval of the massive and controversial arch project, which would sit in Memorial Circle between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.
The District of Columbia and Virginia, who are suing over the project, filed a motion for the temporary restraining order. In an opinion accompanying her order Chutkan said they have demonstrated a likelihood of standing to sue and an immediate harm.
Chutkan wrote in the opinion that “the harm is certain” and that the Trump administration has said it was ready to start construction almost immediately after the commission’s approval.
The commission passed the motion to approve final site building plans 8-4, with the four votes in opposition coming from commissioners who were not appointed by Trump.
Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., whose district includes the cemetery, applauded the ruling and accused Trump of trying to bypass legal barriers.
“This fight is not over. While this decision prevents Donald Trump from immediately implementing his plans to create a monument to his own ego, the courts and Congress must put in place permanent safeguards to stop the Trump Administration from violating the law and proceeding with this project,” Beyer said in a statement.
The Department of Interior and National Park Service did not immediately respond to requests for comment about Chutkan’s order early Friday.
The commission gave the project a green light after a hearing at which scores of area residents lined up to voice their opposition to the project.
Public comment at the hearing lasted more than nine hours, which commission Chair Mark Paoletta said was “more than ever.” The comments mostly related to the impact on Arlington National Cemetery, which is the final resting place of the nation’s fallen service members, as well as the project’s height, scale and safety.
Paoletta, who is general counsel at the Office of Management and Budget and was appointed chairman of the commission in August, said at the meeting that it was a “national disgrace” that such a memorial had not already been built. He also praised Trump’s “monumental vision,” saying it would be “the grandest arch ever built by mankind.”
The virtual meeting was interrupted for around 30 minutes during public comments by what Paoletta said was a “malicious attack” that caused the site to crash. He said it’s the “first time this has ever happened.”
Close to 130 members of the public were signed up to speak.

“We’ll have this thing done, whether it’s past midnight or not,” Paoletta said after the interruption. The vote ended in the 10 p.m. hour.
Reps. Brian Mast, R-Fla., and Andrew Clyde, R-Ga., spoke in favor of the project, while Beyer expressed concern over the project and criticized the Trump administration over the approval process.
The governments of Virginia and the District of Columbia have argued the project is illegal.
They asked a judge to immediately halt any construction in a bid to head off possible legal gamesmanship by the administration, citing its earlier destruction of the East Wing of the White House to build a ballroom that includes national security measures.
“It is entirely foreseeable that, once construction begins, Defendants will argue, as they have done in other cases, that an order halting construction would irreparably harm the federal government, pose security risks, and impermissibly alter the status quo they have unilaterally created,” they said. “The Court should not allow this cynical gambit to succeed.”
Following Thursday’s vote, attorneys for the Justice Department filed a document informing Chutkan, the judge, who had asked to be notified after the commission took action.
Trump has said the arch would celebrate the nation’s 250th anniversary and include a military complex with drones and snipers, which he said would be important for national security. The final plans submitted to the commission, however, did not mention drones, ammunition storage or sniper positions.
Asked about the omission at the hearing, Greg Wischer, deputy chief of staff at the Interior Department, said the current “design is capable of hosting national security functions,” but details of those functions aren’t public and have been filed under seal in the court case.
Preservationists and military veterans first sued to block the project this year, arguing that it needed to be authorized by Congress and that the site was improper.
“Its location on Memorial Circle would situate the monument on an axis between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, obstructing a line of sight that was designed to represent the unification of the Nation following the Civil War and that has existed for nearly a century,” they said.
Testifying at the meeting Thursday, one of the plaintiffs, Vietnam War veteran Michael Lemmon, who was U.S. ambassador to Armenia during the Clinton administration, called the planned arch “frankly blasphemous.”
Virginia and the District of Columbia filed their own action to stop the project last week, contending it “defies at least five federal statutes,” including one that “generally limits buildings in the District to a maximum height of 130 feet.”
The 250-foot arch “would exceed that limit almost twice over.”

title: What new Kane deal means for England and the Premier League record
rawText:
What new Kane deal means for England and the Premier League record
- Published
Harry Kane's decision to sign a new contract with Bayern Munich carries heavy significance for the Bundesliga giants, who have been celebrating his status as a Ballon d'Or winner, but also for England and the Premier League's record books.
Bayern have acted swiftly to secure the 33-year-old on a deal taking him through to 2029 after he was crowned the world's best player, ensuring England's captain and record goalscorer will spend the final peak years of a magnificent career at Allianz Arena.
Kane has written himself into Bayern legend since joining from Spurs for Â£86m in August 2023, scoring 102 goals in 102 Bundesliga matches, winning two league titles and three successive Golden Boot awards.
It is why Bayern could not contemplate his departure as other clubs eyed his next move - and why the announcement Kane is staying casts ripples far beyond Munich.
Does it mean Kane will never grace the Premier League again? And does it mean - far more enticingly - he has his sights set on two more major tournaments and two more chances to grasp the prize that has eluded him at international level?
Former England striker Chris Sutton told BBC Sport: "I certainly think, although you always have to factor fitness issues into all of this, that Harry is more than capable of carrying on for a few years yet, easily.
"People might say his game lacks a little bit of pace, but he's so strong in other areas. He is a world-class all-round player. His finishing isn't going to be affected in any way by his age. He can still link up play and his football brain is first class.
"I don't see his age being such a big deal. You think of pacy players over the years who rely on that part of the game then lose it as they get older. Harry is not one of those. He seems fit and at the peak of his powers with Bayern and England."
Kane's new contract expires shortly before his 36th birthday, certainly raising the prospect the player who left Spurs as the highest scorer in their history with 280 goals in 435 appearances may never grace the Premier League again.
His consummate professionalism, and apparent ability to develop into the complete player with age, means this can never be discounted.
The notion of an emotional return to Spurs at some point has often provided background noise, but now looks increasingly unlikely.
What it surely means is that Alan Shearer will remain the Premier League's highest scorer - who knows what will happen with Erling Haaland as Manchester City await punishment after being found guilty of breaching financial regulations they deny? - and out of Kane's reach.
Shearer scored 260 goals in 441 Premier League matches for Blackburn Rovers and Newcastle United. Kane scored 213 times in 320 league games for Spurs.
With Kane still 47 short of Shearer's record, it would need a spectacular late-career flourish for him to eclipse the Geordie icon's tally to write another entry into the history books, which also have him as England's highest scorer with 91 goals from a record-equalling 125 caps.
What will be of huge interest to Thomas Tuchel - the coach who took him to Bayern and now leads England - is that Kane has delivered a clear indication that Euro 2028, to be played in the UK and Ireland, is firmly in his sights.
And, when this new deal expires, Kane is also only a year away from the 2030 World Cup, to be played in Morocco, Portugal and Spain, with special centenary opening matches held in Uruguay, Argentina, and Paraguay.
This, of course, is a stretch given the inevitable rigours of age, but few who know Kane, who have watched him move to a new level at Bayern, would ever say never to such a driven personality, hiding fierce mental strength and a competitive instinct behind his humble 'anti-superstar' persona.
Sutton said: "Euro 2028 certainly shouldn't be a problem and who knows beyond that? If Harry has got players around him with pace and dynamism, as well as runners in and around him, then his football brain isn't going to change and he can still play a huge part.
"He's such a sharp, quick, thinker. He reads the game superbly, knows where his next pass is going and has shown an ability to drop deep and impact the game.
"Harry just seems to be getting better and more rounded with age. And as for age, just look at someone like Teddy Sheringham. He was playing and scoring goals for West Ham United in the Premier League in his 40s.
"Sheringham was an incredibly talented player with supreme intelligence. Harry Kane falls right into the same category.
"Ronaldo has just retired from international football with Portugal at 41, but he is a totally different player than Harry Kane. Harry is one who can drop a little bit deeper to use his incredible ability and range of passing.
"As well as that ability, it is about how Harry's football brain works as much as anything and that won't change with age."
And it is an argument, and a hope, that is even more pertinent as England still do not possess any other striker or forward who could be considered anywhere near Kane's class or potency.
"When you talk about 2028 or 2030, who are the English strikers coming through to challenge him to take him out of the team?" said Sutton. "There's no-one in his class or effectiveness, or anywhere near it."
What also plays into the argument that Kane cannot be ruled out of such long-term involvement is the manner in which he responded so superbly to what was a disappointing Euro 2024, not only as England lost in the final to Spain but because he looked a jaded shadow of his old self.
Kane looked so out of sorts there was a clamour for him to be replaced by Ollie Watkins, then at Aston Villa. He was substituted in all of England's knockout matches, including after only 61 minutes of that final loss to Spain in Berlin.
And yet, Kane still finished as the tournament's joint top scorer with three goals from seven games.

title: Conferencia ‘mañanera’ de Claudia Sheinbaum hoy 5 de noviembre: Síguela aquí en vivo
rawText:
La presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum encabeza la mañanera de este jueves 5 de noviembre desde Palacio Nacional.
En esta conferencia matutina, la mandataria podría referirse al homicidio de Gabriel Rivas Ríos, regidor de Cuernavaca que había denunciado amenazas de muerte antes de su asesinato el 4 de noviembre.
También podrían posicionarse respecto al intento del exgobernador de Chihuahua, Ernesto ‘N’, para que un juez le permita recibir la pensión del Bienestar; luego que una jurista rechazara un amparo.
Sigue el minuto a minuto de la mañanera de Sheinbaum a través de El Financiero.
¿Qué sucedió en la mañanera de Claudia Sheinbaum el 4 de noviembre?
En la conferencia anterior, la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum celebró la victoria de Xavier Becerra y Gina Hinojosa, ambos hijos de mexicanos inmigrantes, quienes se convirtieron en gobernadores de California y Texas, respectivamente.
La mandataria aseguró que la victoria del Partido Demócrata en las elecciones intermedias de Estados Unidos representaba un “mensaje del pueblo”.
En tanto, subrayó que su gobierno buscará la mejor relación con EU en medio de las negociaciones del T-MEC tras la victoria de los demócratas.
La conferencia se centró en el avance de los Plan Michoacán, una estrategia implementada después del homicidio de Carlos Manzo, que cumplió un año el 1 de noviembre.

title: Mother and daughter killed in grizzly bear attack, Canadian authorities confirm
rawText:
Search teams in Canada have discovered the body of a 20-year-old woman and confirmed that both she and her mother were killed in an attack that conservation officers now believe could have involved multiple grizzly bears.
Late on Tuesday, conservation officers in British Columbia said the two women, who were reported missing over the weekend, were located near a trail a short distance from their home.
The discovery has shaken a community where, earlier in the year, a grizzly attacked a group of schoolchildren and their teachers.
“Our thoughts are with the families of the victims during this tragic time,” Inspector Jeff Tyre of the British Columbia Conservation Officer Service said in a video posted online. Tyre later said the conservation service was investigating the possibility that more than one bear was involved in the fatal attack.
“We appreciate people’s concerns and the desire to assist but it is critical the public stay out of the area – both due to the danger and to allow officers to do their work,” he said.
Jenny Balcarras, an art therapist, and her daughter Selah Reed were reported missing by relatives over the weekend. A family member posted on Facebook about them, later updating it after the conservation service announced the suspected attack to indicate that their vehicle had been found at a trailhead near Bella Coola, British Columbia. Balcarras’s remains were found first and Reed was located a day later.
A fundraiser for Balcarras started by her family mourned a woman who had recently moved to Bella Coola, a community of roughly 2,100 people, for a new job and “to start a new chapter” of her life. She leaves behind three adult children and a grandchild.
“[Jenny] was working toward building a future and had not yet had the opportunity to establish savings or put aside funds to help her family with unexpected expenses such as these,” wrote relative Mary Melissa Smith. “Tragically, no one could have anticipated that her family would be faced with such an unimaginable loss.”
The family also mourned 20-year-old Selah, who had her “whole life ahead of her” before the attack.
“She was only beginning her journey into adulthood, making this loss even more heartbreaking,” wrote Smith.
Both Balcarras and Reed had lived in communities in remote and rugged parts of the province, as well as time in Alaska.
The suspected attack happened at the Snooka West trail area, about 8km (5 miles) east of Bella Coola, on the province’s central coast.
Bella Coola, which sits at the end of a fjord along the province’s central coast, is a remote location, and abundant food sources mean that grizzly bears are a common sight in the region, which is informally known as the Great Bear rainforest.
Grizzly attacks in the province are exceedingly rare, but last November, 11 people, some as young as nine years old, were injured when a grizzly emerged from the forest near 4 Mile, a Nuxalk community, and attacked a school group on a lunch break alongside a walking trail. Despite an extensive search, the bear was never located.
Samuel Schooner, elected chief of the Nuxalk Nation, said on Tuesday: “Our thoughts are with the victim’s family as they learn of this tragic event.” Schooner said a trapping effort to find the bear was under way and asked media to refrain from contacting community members.
The province’s premier-designate, Lorne Doerkson, called the news “heartbreaking” and said he was thinking of the victims’ family and the Nuxalk Nation.
“At a time of such profound grief and uncertainty, my thoughts are with everyone who is hurting and with all those supporting one another through an incredibly difficult day.”

title: NASA is racing against time to save the Hubble Space Telescope
rawText:
NASA is racing against time to save the Hubble Space Telescope
- Date:
- November 4, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- NASA is exploring a daring plan to save the legendary Hubble Space Telescope from its eventual fiery plunge into Earth's atmosphere. After more than 35 years of groundbreaking discoveries, Hubble is slowly losing altitude, and without intervention, it could fall back to Earth as early as 2033 or 2034. To keep the iconic observatory operating, NASA is asking private space companies to propose innovative ways to boost Hubble into a higher orbit, upgrade its capabilities, or safely dispose of it when its mission finally ends.
- Share:
NASA is investigating whether private space companies could help extend the life of the Hubble Space Telescope, which has spent more than 35 years transforming our understanding of the universe.
On October 29, the agency issued a Request for Information seeking details about commercial technologies that could be used to service Hubble while it remains in orbit. The goal is to determine whether new spacecraft capabilities could keep the iconic observatory operating longer, improve its performance, or help bring its mission to a safe conclusion.
"Hubble still has important science ahead of it, and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible," said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. "If there are innovative and cost-effective ways to extend the life of an asset already on orbit, we owe it to the American taxpayer and the scientific community to explore them. Extending Hubble's life would mean more discoveries, more science, and more opportunities to expand our understanding of the universe."
NASA Considers Raising Hubble Into a Higher Orbit
One possibility under consideration is sending a spacecraft to push Hubble into a higher orbit. This could counteract the gradual loss of altitude that threatens the telescope's future and potentially allow it to continue making scientific discoveries for additional years.
NASA is also interested in missions that could service the telescope and improve its capabilities. Another option would focus on safely retiring Hubble when its scientific work is complete, either by guiding it through a controlled descent into Earth's atmosphere or arranging for its disposal in orbit.
These possibilities are being explored rather than formally approved. By reaching out to commercial companies, NASA hopes to better understand what technologies are available and whether they could provide practical, affordable solutions.
"Hubble is a national icon that has fundamentally changed how humanity views our universe for more than 35 years," said Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington. "Commercial industry has rapidly evolved in recent years to offer new capabilities for in-space satellite capture and servicing. Given the time we have until Hubble's anticipated re-entry, we are eager to explore the breadth of possibilities to boost Hubble to a higher orbit while we develop the flagship mission to follow."
Companies interested in participating can review NASA's Request for Information online. The agency is accepting responses until 3 p.m. EST on Monday, November 30.
Why Hubble Could Fall Back to Earth by 2034
Although Hubble continues to operate in space, its orbit is gradually shrinking. The telescope travels through low Earth orbit, where traces of Earth's atmosphere create drag that slowly reduces the altitude of orbiting spacecraft.
Even hundreds of miles above the planet, the atmosphere is not completely absent. The tiny amount of remaining gas produces resistance as spacecraft move through it. Over long periods, this effect can cause satellites to lose altitude and eventually descend into denser layers of the atmosphere.
Unlike spacecraft equipped with engines that can periodically raise their orbits, Hubble has no propulsion system capable of maintaining its altitude. Without outside assistance, it cannot reverse this gradual orbital decline.
NASA's current analysis suggests that Hubble will likely reenter Earth's atmosphere sometime between 2033 and 2034. To prevent that outcome through an orbital boost, the agency expects that a mission would need to occur by 2032.
That timeline leaves a limited window to evaluate potential solutions, develop a mission, and carry it out before the telescope descends too far.
Extending Hubble's Legacy of Cosmic Discoveries
Since beginning operations more than three decades ago, Hubble has become one of the most influential scientific observatories ever launched. Its observations have helped reshape astronomers' understanding of the cosmos, and the telescope continues to produce discoveries that advance research across many areas of astronomy.
Hubble is also the product of a longstanding international partnership between NASA and ESA (European Space Agency).
NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, oversees the telescope and its mission operations, with additional operational support from Denver-based Lockheed Martin Space.
Scientific operations are handled by the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, which is operated by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy on NASA's behalf.
With commercial spaceflight technology advancing, NASA is now evaluating whether Hubble could benefit from capabilities that were not available when it was originally designed. A successful mission to raise its orbit or enhance its systems could allow the historic telescope to continue exploring the universe well beyond its currently projected orbital lifetime.

title: SLAC scientists find conclusive proof of a mysterious third type of magnetism
rawText:
SLAC scientists find conclusive proof of a mysterious third type of magnetism
- Date:
- November 4, 2026
- Source:
- SLAC
- Summary:
- For nearly 90 years, scientists believed magnetism fell into just two categories, but researchers have now confirmed a remarkable third type called altermagnetism. Using specialized X-rays, they uncovered a unique magnetic signature that proves these materials behave differently from conventional magnets. Altermagnets combine stability with the ability to efficiently carry information, potentially overcoming major limitations in today's electronics. The discovery could lead to faster computers, more efficient data centers, and breakthroughs in quantum technology.
- Share:
For nearly 90 years, physicists have divided magnetic materials into two main categories: ferromagnets and antiferromagnets. Now, scientists have confirmed that a third type exists, revealing a previously unrecognized form of magnetic behavior that could lead to major advances in computing and electronics.
The breakthrough comes from a research team led by the U.S. Department of Energy's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. In a study published in Science, the researchers presented compelling experimental evidence for altermagnetism, a distinct magnetic phase that combines important characteristics of the two traditionally recognized types.
"In the past few years, scientists have observed phenomena that don't fit neatly into the ferromagnetism-antiferromagnetism dichotomy," explained lead author Daniel Jost, associate scientist at SLAC and Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences. "Researchers have been compiling evidence of a third type of magnetism that bridges the qualities of these two classes. We believe our results provide robust experimental confirmation that this third phase -- altermagnetism -- is real."
The team focused on manganese telluride (MnTe), a material that had long been classified as an antiferromagnet. Building on earlier research, the scientists identified direct evidence of chirality, a distinctive asymmetry in the material's magnetic structure. This property resembles the way a spiral staircase or screw twists in a particular direction and provides a crucial signature of altermagnetism.
Beyond its importance for fundamental physics, the finding could help researchers develop magnetic materials with properties suited to future technologies, including advanced memory systems, quantum devices, and more energy-efficient data centers.
Understanding the Two Traditional Types of Magnetism
Magnetism is familiar from everyday experiences, whether it is a refrigerator magnet holding up a photograph or a compass aligning with Earth's magnetic field. But the physics behind these effects is far more complicated than it appears.
At the atomic level, magnetism is connected to a quantum property of electrons known as spin. Although spin is not literally an electron rotating like a tiny ball, it behaves in certain ways as though the electron has its own angular momentum. Scientists commonly describe the two possible spin orientations as "up" and "down."
When these spins become organized into particular patterns, a material can exhibit magnetic properties. However, that does not necessarily mean it will produce an externally detectable magnetic field.
In ferromagnetic materials, electron spins align in the same direction (up-up-up or down-down-down). Their combined effect produces the familiar magnetic field associated with ordinary magnets. People have used materials with this behavior for thousands of years.
A second category, identified in 1933, works differently. In antiferromagnets, neighboring electron spins point in opposite directions (up-down-up-down). Because the magnetic contributions oppose one another, they cancel out, leaving no overall magnetization.
A Third Type of Magnetism Challenges the Old Rules
For almost nine decades, these two categories provided the basic framework for understanding how magnetic order arises in materials. However, experimental observations in recent years began revealing behavior that neither category could fully explain.
Some materials displayed alternating electron spins and no overall magnetization, just like antiferromagnets. Yet they could also support useful spin currents, a property associated with ferromagnetic behavior. Spin currents allow information to be carried through the spin properties of electrons rather than relying entirely on their electrical charge.
The unusual combination suggested that scientists were dealing with something fundamentally different. In 2022, researchers introduced the term "altermagnets" for materials belonging to this proposed third magnetic class.
The key difference lies in the arrangement of atoms within the material. Altermagnets have alternating spin orientations (up-down-up-down), but the crystal structures surrounding the oppositely aligned spins are rotated relative to one another.
This rotation breaks a form of symmetry that exists in conventional antiferromagnets. Although the distinction is subtle, it can dramatically change how electrons behave, allowing altermagnets to combine properties once considered incompatible.
Scientists Find the Missing Evidence for Altermagnetism
Even as experimental support for altermagnetism accumulated, researchers still needed a decisive way to establish that it represented a genuinely distinct magnetic phase.
"By 2024, there were some factors that spoke strongly in favor of altermagnetism being real," Jost said, "but there was still a missing piece to the puzzle."
That missing evidence involved chirality, a property sometimes described as "handedness." An object is chiral when its mirror image cannot be perfectly aligned with the original. Human hands provide a simple example: Your left and right hands are mirror images, but a left hand cannot fit properly into a right-handed glove.

title: One dead and another missing in suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada
rawText:
A mother is dead and her daughter is missing in western Canada after a suspected grizzly bear attack in the same community where a bear attacked a group of schoolchildren earlier in the year.
On Tuesday, the British Columbia conservation officer service said in a social media post that it had launched a search for the two missing people on the weekend, and that during the search on Sunday an officer found the mother’s body. The search for her 19-year-old daughter is ongoing.
“Our thoughts are with the families of the victims during this tragic time,” Inspector Jeff Tyre said in a video posted online.
Jenny Balcarras, an art therapist, and her daughter were reported missing by relatives over the weekend. A family member posted on Facebook about them, later updating it after the conservation service announced the suspected attack to indicate that their vehicle had been found at a trailhead near Bella Coola, British Columbia.
The suspected attack happened at the Snooka West trail area, about 8km (4.97 miles) east of Bella Coola, on the province’s central coast.
Bella Coola, a community of roughly 2,100 people, sits at the end of a fjord along the province’s central coast. Its remote location and abundant food sources mean that grizzly bears are a common sight in the region, which is informally known as the Great Bear rainforest.
Grizzly attacks in the province are exceedingly rare, but last November, 11 people, some as young as nine years old, were injured when a grizzly emerged from the forest near 4 Mile, a Nuxalk community, and attacked a school group on a lunch break alongside a walking trail. Despite an extensive search, the bear was never located.
“While the full circumstances are still unfolding, we understand first-hand the trauma this incident will inflict upon the victims’ family members, the victims of last year’s attack and the community at large,” said Samuel Schooner, elected chief of the Nuxalk Nation, on Tuesday. “Our thoughts are with the victim’s family as they learn of this tragic event.”
Schooner said a trapping effort to find the bear was under way and asked media to refrain from contacting community members.

title: Fossilised red blood cells found in 115m-year-old dinosaur’s bone, say scientists
rawText:
It could be the opening of a Jurassic Park rip-off: scientists examining ancient dinosaur bones find what appear to be fossilised red blood cells, and traces of the molecule that gives the beast’s blood its distinctive crimson hue.
But that is what researchers are claiming to have discovered after analysing the hind leg bones of a small, meat-eating dinosaur called an Aratasaurus that lived and died in what is now north-eastern Brazil 115m years ago.
Electron microscope images of the dinosaur bones revealed small, round structures that resemble red blood cells in fine channels where blood vessels once ran, while chemical tests identified the presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around the body.
Such claims are controversial because biological tissues and molecules can break down fast, leaving little or no trace in ancient fossils. But if confirmed, it would open up entirely new avenues for scientists, allowing them to investigate dinosaur blood, metabolism and even their activity levels.
“We are seeing a mineral and molecular echo of the dinosaur’s original biology,” said Prof Kliti Grice at Curtin University in Western Australia who led the research team. “Fossilised red blood cells with distinct chemistry related to heme have never been found in situ in any fossil, let alone a dinosaur. This is a world first.”
The fossilised remnants of the Aratasaurus were discovered in a mine in 2008 and have since been held in the National Museum of Brazil, where researchers continue to study them. While analysing the dinosaur’s hind leg bones, Grice spotted the structures that resembled red blood cells.
The scientists’ suspicions that they were looking at red blood cells were bolstered when chemical tests came back positive for heme and its breakdown products. Tests also found traces of the amino acid building blocks for collagen, a key protein in connective and other tissues.
If the structures really are fossilised red blood cells, as the researchers contend, it raises the question of how they were preserved. According to Grice, a manganese compound called hausmannite, which formed in and around the blood cells, may have lent a helping hand by stabilising them prior to fossilisation. The same process might have helped preserve the amino acids, she added. The study appears in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
The work is already stoking debate. Prof Mary Schweitzer at North Carolina State University in the US, who has discovered remnants of blood vessels and soft tissues in dinosaur fossils, is not convinced Grice and her colleagues have found red blood cells. One reason for her doubt is that the dinosaur’s red blood cells should have a “nuclear bulge” making them appear dome-like on both sides. The structures Grice found are concave, suggesting they might be something else.
Schweitzer was more persuaded by the discovery of heme and collagen amino acids in the bone and said there was so much more to learn from exceptionally well-preserved fossils. Schweitzer added: “The conventional wisdom in palaeontology that all endogenous organics would disappear in a million years or less is being routinely challenged, and will continue to be as technological approaches to palaeontological specimens are more routinely applied.”
Another question the research raises is what other biological material might lurk in fossils collections around the world. On this, Grice urges extreme caution, adding that her work does not imply that large biological molecules such as proteins or DNA live on in ancient fossils. “Any extraordinary claim needs extraordinary analytical evidence,” she said. “The aim isn’t to find Jurassic Park DNA, it’s to determine how much genuine molecular information deep time can preserve.”
“The really exciting implication is that extraordinary molecular information may already be sitting in museum collections around the world, waiting for us to ask new questions of old fossils,” she added.

title: UK was ‘vehement’ slavery reparations should not be on Commonwealth summit agenda
rawText:
British officials reportedly insisted that discussions of reparations for slavery should not be on the agenda of the Commonwealth leaders’ summit in Antigua and Barbuda – and even warned that Andy Burnham would not attend the meeting if the subject was formally included, according to a leading Caribbean political figure.
Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure in the reparatory justice movement Repair Campaign, welcomed Britain’s decision to enter structured dialogue on reparations, but said the UK had come “kicking and screaming” to the conversation.
Currently, slavery reparations is not on the official agenda of the Commonwealth Heads of Government (Chogm) summit, which begins on Sunday.
Trade, climate resilience and finance, sustainable debt, democracy and investment in opportunities for young people are among the stated priorities for the 56-nation bloc spanning Africa, Asia, the Caribbean and the Americas, the Pacific and Europe.
“My understanding from informed circles is that Britain was vehement not to have the matter on the agenda. The British officials – and in that regard they were joined by the Canadian officials – were even raising the prospect that if it is on the agenda the prime minister of Britain wouldn’t go,” Gonsalves told the Guardian.
“They also started to circulate this untruth that India didn’t want it on the agenda, but that was not so at all. India was very supportive at the UN general assembly resolution on March 25th, 2026. So they were spreading this false word about India.”
Gonsalves said that the relentless campaign by Caribbean nations, amplified by a growing regional and global reparations movement, has propelled reparatory justice to the heart of the political conversation at the meeting.
“Because of what happened at the UN, because of what happened in Africa, what happened in the Caribbean, and all the work which is taking place in Britain itself too, inside of the British parliament, inside of the British Labour party, both in the Commons and the House of Lords, it is an issue which you can’t duck any more,” he said.
He added: “The danger of not putting it formally on the agenda is what we see happening now, that everybody who could have foreseen, whether or not it’s formally on the agenda, even the nature of how the discussions take place at the Commonwealth, and certainly in the retreats, it would have been raised.”
Gonsalves said while the actual structured dialoguewas unlikely to happen at Chogm, it was expected that when the leaders met in their private retreat, the format and details of the dialogue would be discussed.
He said: “The British government, they’re coming, kicking and screaming to the table of structured dialogue. But at least they’re coming.”
An FCDO spokesperson said: “We categorically reject this completely untrue accusation. The UK has approached this conversation in good faith, and we have at no point told any other Chogm member what should not be on an agenda.
“Our position on reparations is clear but this government respects the right of others to raise matters as they wish.”
Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, chair of the Caribbean Community (Caricom) Reparations Commission, had described the meeting as “the Chogm of reparations”, adding that reparatory justice was “the number one item” for the Caribbean as Commonwealth leaders gather in the region.
On Friday there was a historic shift in Britain’s position when the British prime minister went further than any of his predecessors by agreeing to structured dialogue and to consider an apology.
Though Caribbean governments and campaigners welcomed Burnham’s announcement, made in an op-ed for the Guardian, it was clear that agreeing on forms of reparations was still a priority for the region.
Guyana’s president, Irfaan Ali, welcomed Burnham’s statement and called for a Commonwealth subcommittee to work out the details of the dialogue over the next six to 12 months.
“I’m happy that finally the discourse has moved to a position where it should have been, where the British government is involved, because that’s the state we are dealing with,” he said.
Ali said the talks should move beyond attempting to put a price on the indignity of slavery and towards addressing its developmental consequences.
“How do we identify a system of support where the UK government, with its financial institutions, can sit with countries … and work on a development pathway, identify development gaps, whether in health, education, social services, infrastructure?”
Barbados’s prime minister, Mia Mottley, thanked Burnham for “breaking new ground”, while making clear that the two sides remained divided. “On reparations in particular, our views differ, and we will say so plainly and respectfully,” she said.
Mottley identified an apology, investment in health and education, tackling systemic poverty and inequality, and fairer debt terms among areas where agreement could be reached.
The Bahamas prime minister, Philip Davis, said the talks were not simply about “historical remembrance” but “the enduring consequences of slavery and the importance of justice, acknowledgment and meaningful redress”.
As the meeting kicks off on Sunday, the 45th anniversary of Antigua and Barbuda’s independence from British colonial rule, King Charles is indicating he will not follow Burnham and offer a full apology, there is still a sense that the reparations fight is far from over.
King Charles and Burnham will be greeted with protests as they travel through Antigua’s capital, St John’s, to attend Chogm events.
On billboards, placards and T-shirts, in letters and at a candlelight vigil for the thousands of Africans trafficked to Antigua and Barbuda during the transatlantic slave trade, the message from the Caribbean will be clear: there will be calls for an apology and reparations.

title: Poll: Voters demand change and a check on Trump, fueling a steep Democratic midterm advantage
rawText:
Democrats have a sizable advantage in the battle for control of Congress days ahead of the midterm elections, a new national NBC News poll finds, with voters clamoring for change and voicing all-time high disapproval of President Donald Trump.
Registered voters prefer a Democratic-controlled Congress by a 7-point margin, with Democrats leading Republicans 52%-45% — 2 points more than in last month’s poll. That includes a 21-point lead among independents.
Three percent of voters remained undecided as the poll was conducted from Oct. 28 to Oct. 30, and how they shift in the final days could tilt the outcome in dead-heat House and Senate races around the country. While the overall poll suggests that Democrats are poised to capitalize on a well of dissatisfaction with the president and his policies, there are findings that complicate the favorable picture.
When it comes to which party better handles key issues, voters give Republicans and Democrats about even marks, and the Democratic Party remains deeply unpopular. Meanwhile, Republican voters in GOP-held districts and in states Trump won in 2024 are sticking with their party — which is notable because much of the battle for control of both the House and Senate runs through this red terrain.
But there are also numerous signs of trouble for the GOP, with Trump at the center of a difficult political environment for Republicans and their slim majorities in both houses of Congress. The president’s disapproval rating has climbed to 60%, a new high mark in the NBC News poll across his two terms, and his approval rating stands at 40%.
After Trump won a second term in 2024 promising to bring down prices and restore the economic conditions of his first term, roughly 3 in 4 voters head into the midterms dissatisfied with the state of the economy. Nearly two-thirds of voters are calling for a change from the direction Trump has been leading the country, with 50% calling for “a great deal” of change, a new high mark in NBC News polling data.
And for the first time in 30 years of NBC News polling, more voters say they are dissatisfied with their financial situation (51%) than satisfied (49%).
“The Trump presidency can be summarized as the promise of two years ago and the peril of two days from now,” said Democratic pollster Jeff Horwitt of Hart Research Associates, who conducted the survey with Republican pollster Bill McInturff of Public Opinion Strategies.
Horwitt noted Trump returned to the White House after promising economic prosperity and peace. But now voters are expressing widespread concerns about the economy, with prices rising during the Iran war.
Amid those concerns, 64% of voters — including a third of Trump voters — say the president has fallen short of their expectations, with 34% saying he has lived up to them. Seventy percent of voters say the country is on the wrong track, a 9-point increase over the last year.
Voters continue to rank inflation and the cost of living as the most important issues facing the country, followed by government corruption, threats to democracy and immigration and border security.
“Democrats are in total control of the 2026 issue agenda,” said McInturff, the Republican pollster, noting that only voters who think immigration is a top issue are breaking for his party right now.
Democrats have a 1-point advantage on which party would better control inflation, a slight decline from September but still a warning sign for the GOP, which led on the issue in 2024. Republicans have a 2-point advantage on the economy, a marked decline from the party’s double-digit advantage on the issue in recent years.
Voters are also signaling that they are fired up about the midterms, with 70% ranking themselves as a “9” or “10” on a 10-point scale of interest in the election. Democrats have a 12-point advantage among those most-engaged voters, while Republicans have a 2-point edge among voters who are less interested in the election.
Self-described MAGA Republicans also say they’re significantly more interested in the election than Republicans who don’t identify with the MAGA wing, as Trump and his party push to turn out voters who typically sit out midterm elections.
That dynamic could be one reason why Republicans have leaned into culture war arguments in key races, attacking Democrats on transgender issues. The new poll shows a potential limitation of that strategy: Democrats have a 5-point advantage on the question of which party would better handle transgender issues, despite those Republican attacks.
It’s not all good news for Democrats, and the poll contains fresh signs that a number of voters are pushing back on the GOP, as opposed to falling in love with the Democratic Party, which remains deeply unpopular.
Just 29% of voters view the Democratic Party positively, while 38% have positive views of the Republican Party. Around half of voters have negative views of both parties.
Still, some voters who are wary of Democrats are still planning to support them this year.
“Republicans have proven that they are not to be trusted. So I would rather see the balance of power shift, than maintain one party’s control,” one poll respondent from Texas, who voted for Trump in 2024 and is supporting Democrats for Congress this year, said in an expanded response.
“I don’t trust Republicans or Democrats, really,” the man added.
Republican disappointment
Frustrations among voters like that man from Texas, who backed Trump in 2024 and typically backs Republicans, are dragging down the president and GOP candidates this year.
Republicans are torn on whether the country is moving in the right direction (48%), or the wrong direction (43%). One year ago, Republicans said the country was going in the right direction, 75%-24%.
Now, a majority of Republicans (53%) are dissatisfied with the state of the economy. And 37% of Trump’s own party believe he’s fallen short of his promises.
